title: CONGENITAL MYOPATHY 10B, MILD VARIANT
alt_titles: MYOPATHY, AREFLEXIA, RESPIRATORY DISTRESS, AND DYSPHAGIA, EARLY-ONSET, MILD VARIANT

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that the mild variant of congenital myopathy-10 (CMYO10B) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the MEGF10 gene (612453) on chromosome 5q23.

paragraphs.text: The mild variant of congenital myopathy-10 (CMYO10B) is an autosomal recessive myopathy. Onset is usually in infancy or childhood, and some cases begin in adulthood. Features include axial and proximal muscle weakness, facial weakness, contractures, scoliosis, hypernasal speech and respiratory insufficiency that develops later than in the classic early-onset form. Muscle biopsy often shows minicores. Reported patients have mostly carried missense mutations, and the disease is milder than in patients with null mutations in MEGF10.

paragraphs.text: Boyden et al. (2012) studied a nonconsanguineous Caucasian family of mixed European ancestry (family 1030) in which 3 of 4 sibs had an undiagnosed autosomal recessive myopathy that resembled multiminicore disease in some respects. Onset was by 12 months of age with neck weakness, and neck contractures were present in infancy. The weakness was mainly axial and proximal, and the patients also had facial weakness. They had contractures of the elbows, knees and heel cords, and serum creatine kinase was mildly elevated. All 3 patients had childhood-onset scoliosis treated with spinal fusion surgery. Beginning at age 10 to 11 years, all 3 developed respiratory problems that were treated with bilevel positive airway pressure ventilation at night. All 3 had hypernasal speech, 1 had a cleft palate, and some had neck muscle atrophy. Muscle biopsy showed fatty replacement, increased endomysial connective tissue, minicores, variation in fiber size and type I fiber predominance. There were no rimmed vacuoles, nemaline rods, central cores or ragged red fibers.

paragraphs.text: Croci et al. (2022) reported a 22-year-old Italian man born to healthy consanguineous parents with no family history of neuromuscular disease. From the first months of life he had weak suction and axial hypotonia. Motor development was not delayed and he did not have intellectual disability. He developed slowly progressive muscle weakness with impaired walking, elbow and ankle contractures, equinovarus foot stance, scoliosis and hyperlordosis. He also had rhinolalia, dysphagia, and respiratory involvement that required nocturnal noninvasive ventilation, with recurrent pulmonary infections due to aspiration. Examination showed generalized muscular hypotrophy, cleft palate and global areflexia. There was no facial weakness and sensation was not impaired. Nerve conduction studies showed reduced amplitude of muscle evoked potentials. Muscle biopsy showed fiber size variation, internal nuclei, fibrosis, whorled fibers, cytoplasmic inclusions and minicores. His first muscle biopsy showed only nonspecific changes, and the myofibrillar changes with minicores were seen in a later biopsy.

paragraphs.text: In the 3 affected sibs of family 1030, Boyden et al. (2012) identified compound heterozygous missense mutations in the MEGF10 gene: c.976T-C (C326R) and c.2320T-C (C774R). MEGF10 was the sole remaining candidate gene in the linkage regions. Sanger sequencing confirmed that the mutations were in trans in the affected sibs and segregated with the myopathy in all 6 family members. The mutations were absent from 715 and 645 control subjects, respectively, and both affected cysteine residues were conserved in all 43 species examined.

paragraphs.text: Boyden et al. (2012) also screened the entire MEGF10 open reading frame in 190 patients with unexplained myopathies and selected exons in another 82. Only 1 patient carried a mutation: a heterozygous c.211C-T (R71W) change. She was a Caucasian girl of distant Portuguese ancestry who had been diagnosed with multiminicore disease and was the only affected member of her family. She presented at several weeks of age with hypotonia, a weak neck and a floppy head. She also had a markedly high arched palate, failure to thrive due to poor feeding, blue-tinged sclerae, hyperflexible joints, frequent pulmonary infections in childhood, mild scoliosis, facial weakness, and mild nonprogressive proximal weakness. Her serum CK was mildly elevated (302 U/L). Muscle biopsy showed minicores, confirmed by electron microscopy, together with internalized nuclei and marked variation in fiber size. The variant was also present in the heterozygous state in an unaffected parent, so it had not arisen de novo, and no second mutation was found.

paragraphs.text: In a 22-year-old Italian man with CMYO10B born to consanguineous parents, Croci et al. (2022) identified a homozygous c.2096G-C transversion (NM_001256545.2) in the MEGF10 gene, resulting in a cys699-to-ser (C699S) substitution in an EGF-like domain. The mutation was found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, and both healthy parents were heterozygous carriers. The patient had early-onset, slowly progressive myopathy with minicores and myofibrillar changes on muscle biopsy.

checks.evidence_quote: we found a new likely pathogenic mutation in MEGF10, which is responsible for a progressive form of mvEMARDD with myofibrillar alterations at muscle biopsy
